Four Major Division of RStudio GUI

Keyboard Shortcuts

The best way to “enjoy” and gain more when using RStudio GUI is to master some basic keyboard shortcuts.

Note: The + (plus) symbol in the following “key-shortcuts” means to hold the keys in sequence without letting go of the (previous) ones before it.

Accessing Some Panes and Managing Overall GUI Size

  1. Ctrl + 1 – Source
  2. Ctrl + 2 – Console
  3. Ctrl + 3 – Help
  4. Ctrl + 4 – History
  5. Ctrl + 5 – Files
  6. Ctrl + 6 – Plots
  7. Ctrl + 7 – Packages
  8. Ctrl + 8 – Environment
  9. Ctrl + 9 – Viewer
  10. Ctrl + 0 – Reset to default GUI overall size (100%)
  11. Ctrl + Minus – Reduce GUI overall size (<100%)
  12. Ctrl + Plus – Increase GUI overall size (>100%)

Full-screen on a Specific Pane

To zoom in (full-screen) on a specific pane, just add a Shift in the key shortcuts above.

For example, to ‘full-screen’ the Console pane, just press Ctrl + Shift + 2.

To undo the ‘full-screen’, just press the same keys, which in the current example is Ctrl + Shift + 2.

Some other frequently and equally-important keyboard shortcuts

  1. Ctrl + Shift + H – Quickly set or change the current working directory.
  2. Ctrl + Shift + K – Knit/Build a RMD/QMD file.
  3. Ctrl + Enter – To run one or several R script line(s) of code.
  4. Ctrl + Shift + Enter – To run a code chunk within a RMD/QMD file.
  5. Ctrl + Shift + M – To insert a pipe %>% (or |> ) symbol
  6. Alt + Minus – Insert a left-arrow assignment <-
  7. Ctrl + L – To clear the console.
  8. Ctrl + O (letter-Oh) – Open a local file.
  9. Ctrl + Shit + O (letter-Oh) – View the TOC/Outline of a current QMD/RMD file.
  10. Ctrl + F – To find a specific text within an opened file in the Source pane.
  11. Ctrl + Shift + F4 – Toggle between Visual and Source viewing of a QMD/RMD file.
  12. Ctrl + B (bold font), Ctrl + I (italic font), Ctrl + U (underline) – useful for editing in Visual mode only.
  13. Ctrl + / – Insert miscellaneous things (figure, caption, table, etc) within a QMD file while in Visual mode only
  14. Ctrl + X (cut), Ctrl + V (paste)
  15. Ctrl + Z (undo), Ctrl + Shift + Z (redo).
  16. Alt + ArrowUp/Down (PgUp/Down) – move one or several lines of codes in Source viewing mode only
  17. Alt + Shift + ArrowUp/Down (PgUp/Down) – duplicate one or several lines of codes in Source viewing mode only

File Management via RStudio Project

An R project is simply a (named) folder in your local computer that has the following attributes:

  1. It is a folder marked by RStudio as it contains the file called <NameOfProject>.Rproj matching the name of the folder and the project.
  2. Clicking <NameOfProject>.Rproj file will open RStudio and automatically sets the current working directory on that folder.
  3. Any files and sub-folder (such as research data and other relevant documents crucial to your research project) that are within this project folder can readily be accessed whenever you press Ctrl + O (letter-Oh).
Tip

It is highly recommended that one research project should have one R project folder only. If the research project is so large, try creating meaningful sub-projects within the main R project.

Advantages

Creating “Projects” in R has the following advantages:

  1. Focus. It helps you focus on what’s important with one “R data analysis project” at a time.
  2. Declutter. It keeps things (folders, files, etc) in a “clean” and proper order, i.e. avoid file clutter.
  3. Minimize the “Where’s-My-Workding-Directory” hassle. It is time-efficient as it eliminates the hassle of locating or setting your working directory.
  4. Ease of Access. Whenever you open RStudio, it will automatically open the most recent R project you used. If it’s not, you can navigate the project history tab located at the upper-right corner (up to 10 most recent):

Disadvantages

Virtually none as it only takes a few seconds to setup.

Creating RStudio Projects

There are at least three ways to create an R project in RStudio. The ‘fastest’ GUI-friendly way to create it is as follows:

  1. Click the “plus-blue-cube” located at the upper-left corner of the RStudio GUI.
  1. Wait for the following window prompt called New Project Wizard to pop-up.
  1. Decide which among the three options are you going to create your R project.
    1. New Directory. If you are creating an R project from “scratch”, i.e. you don’t have any files yet and just want to create a folder that is marked by RStudio for now. This is useful when creating sub-projects in cases where your research project is so large. (See instructions below on how to set this up.)
    2. Existing Directory. If you already have a folder containing your research files (data, images, etc) and you just want RStudio to mark this folder as your R project.
    3. Version Control. If you have a Github repository (owned by you or possibly from other researchers) and you want it be loaded locally on your RStudio.
Case 1: New Directory

  1. Click “New Directory” option.

  2. Click the “New Project”.

  3. Under the “Create project as subdirectory of” entry, choose which folder your current project will be saved. This could be your large research project under which you want to create a smaller sub-project or it could just another plain folder where you feel secure to save the current new project. The selection is done by clicking the “Browse” button. Next, under the “Directory name”, write the name of the project (or sub-project). Note that this name will be the final name of your project so be sure to name it properly. (Tips: Don’t use special characters but rather use alphanumeric only including space and dash (-); Avoid using lengthy names but rather (not too) short name that captures the essence of the project while at the same differentiating it from other similar projects. Indicating the year the research is/was conducted might be helpful.)


  4. Hit the “Create Project” button and this will restart your RStudio to set the working directory to the new project. If you don’t want to close the currently opened RStudio session while opening the new project, you need to opt to check the “Open in new session” option found at the lower-left corner of the “New Project Wizard” window. (Note: Opening many RStudio sessions might not be advisable if you are running in a low capacity computer as it consumes much of your computer’s RAM.)

Case 2: Existing Directory

  1. Click “Existing Directory”.

  2. Click “Browse” button and navigate to the folder you want to assign as the project folder. Note that name of the project is automatically the name of the folder you are going to choose as the directory folder. Next, click “Create Project” button. If you don’t want to close the current RStudio session, you can opt to check the “Open in new session”. As noted before, opening several sessions in a low capacity computer is not advisable as it consumes to much RAM.

Case 3: Version Control

Before we could use the following version control option using Github, ensure that Git is installed in your as instructed in Installing Git Version Control.

To check the version of Git, open the terminal via Shift + Alt + M and type the following.

git --version

If a git version is shown, it means that there’s an installed git in your system.

Now, let’s try downloading the materials for this day 1 training via using version control from Github. We use the following instructions:

  1. Copy the git project link from the Github respository.

  2. Choose the “Version Control” in RStudio.

  3. Choose “Git” version control option.

  4. Paste the git project link on the input box named “Repository URL”.

  5. It should automatically fill the name of the “Project directory name” right after you paste git URL (link). This name is the name of the folder that RStudio will create in which the downloaded Github repository files are saved. Furthermore, this folder will be saved within the folder path stated under the “Create project as subdirectory of” box. Change this folder path according to your needs if necessary.

  6. Hit the “Create Project” (along with the consideration of possibly opening it in a new session). This will open a “Background Jobs” window which provides you the download and creation progress of the local version of the Github repository. Right after this, depending on whether you opt to open in a session, either a new RStudio session will open the project or the current session is restarted to open the new “cloned” Github repository.
